beats.narration_text: Ciao, this is Liam, in for Bear. Jow-hway Lee's Dusk Duel is a 2D fighting game. Assignment three gives it three simple 3D props: a stone lantern, a training post and a tie-koh drum. Claude built them in Blender through the Blender M C P, and Godot measured them. This film follows what the numbers proved, and what only an eye caught.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW. The corrected misconception is the assignment's own warning: a passing check shows the props arrived at the measured size, not that they look right. BrutalistHesitantWriter replaces every matching token, so 'look' appears once in the text.

beats.narration_text: Here they are in Godot, in a small 3D room beside the 2D game. The lantern frames the arena's edge, like the courtyard's lanterns. The mah-kee-wah-rah is Ah-kah-ken's punching post, its pad at fist height. The tie-koh is the drum you hear in the music loop. The grey box is Ah-kah-ken: one point seven metres.

beats.narration_text: Before Blender held a single prop, the brief was committed: width, depth and height in metres, the origin at the centre of the underside, a triangle budget, base colours, and seven ways it could go wrong. A default thirty-two segment cylinder alone costs a hundred and twenty-four triangles, so every segment count is written down.

beats.narration_text: That's failure case three, predicted in the brief. Joining the parts kept the base bar's origin, three centimetres up. Blender's scene report still said on ground, because it measures the world box. Claude moved the mesh, not the object, so the origin sits at the centre of the underside. Left, Blender after the fix. beats.narration_text: In Godot, the prop room is a plain scene file. Each G L B comes in as an instance at y zero, the top of the floor, spaced along x. Nothing is scaled or rotated here, so any fix had to happen in Blender. The last node is the one point seven metre reference box, centred at point eight five.

beats.narration_text: The headless check takes the bounding box of each prop. Line seventy-two measures the lowest point from the prop's own node, so it can never fail just because the prop floats. Line seventy-nine measures from the floor's top face, read from the Floor node itself, and line eighty-one keeps that gap within a centimetre.

show.event: line 72 highlights: min y: relative to the prop itself
line 79 highlights: relative to the floor

props.title: Two Ways To Ask: On The Floor?
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · godot/tests/check_props3d.gd lines 72-81 · source 1e88b83
props.code:
var min_y := box.position.y - prop.global_position.y
		print("    size %.3f x %.3f x %.3f (x, y, z)  min y %.4f  tris %d  albedo %s"
				% [size.x, size.y, size.z, min_y, tris, hexes])
		for axis in 3:
			check(absf(size[axis] - spec.size[axis]) <= TOL,
					"size axis %d = %.3f, brief %.2f" % [axis, size[axis], spec.size[axis]])
		check(absf(min_y) <= 0.01, "min y %.4f is 0.00 +- 0.01" % min_y)
		var gap := box.position.y - floor_top
		print("    lowest point %.4f m above the floor top (negative = sunk)" % gap)
		check(absf(gap) <= 0.01, "sits on the floor (gap %.4f)" % gap)

cues.label: min y: relative to the prop itself

beats.narration_text: To prove it could fail, Claude raised the tie-koh five centimetres in a copy of the scene. The shadow comes off the base, and the check fails: gap point zero five. The older line seventy-two assertion passed anyway. That's the trap this assignment warns about: a check can prove less than it claims.

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole headless run against the brief. Every dimension lands with zero deviation. Blender's Z becomes Godot's Y through the exporter's plus-Y-up setting, scale is one, rotation zero, and every base colour comes back as the brief's exact hex. Forty-nine checks, none failed. None of that says the props look right.

beats.narration_text: The first eye was Blender's look tool. The mah-kee-wah-rah passed every number, but its round rope bands stood four centimetres out: more collar than rope. Claude then offered an ellipse that could never enclose the pad, and caught that before building. Jow-hway chose chamfered rings instead: same ninety-two triangles, one and a half centimetres out.

beats.narration_text: Then the hand edit. Jow-hway edited the tie-koh with the mouse, in Edit Mode. It nudged the drum body about a centimetre, and flattened the front drumhead onto the body. Asked to fix it, Jow-hway typed this: I can't really fix it, you fix it. Claude put the head back, in two calls, because the first only fixed half.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Checked: size within two centimetres, origin, transforms, budget and colours, forty-nine headless checks with none failed, plus one human look. Uncertain: whether the props suit the game's style and lighting. Claude got four things wrong: the tie-koh origin, an ellipse that couldn't fit, a floor check that couldn't fail, and one call per prop where the course asked for one per object. Jow-hway chose the props, approved the numbers, edited by hand and looked; Claude built, checked and repaired. Next step: deepen the tie-koh's stand.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: Please use Walker to add one simple 3D prop to my game through the Blender MCP. First write its size in metres, its origin, a triangle budget and three predicted failures in my brief, and commit it. Build it one object per call, then write a Godot check that measures it against the floor, and prove that check fails when I raise the prop. The last step is the point: a check you have never seen fail hasn't shown you anything yet. Liam, in for Bear.
